name: Act of March 3, 1875 reducing the Moapa River Reservation to 1,000 acres
citation: Act of Congress of March 3, 1875 (statute page unconfirmed; Royce cessions 576 and 577)
nations: Moapa Band of Paiute Indians (Southern Paiute)
promises: Not a treaty: an Act of Congress. It undid the executive orders of March 12, 1873 and February 12, 1874 that set apart the Moapa River Reservation, directing that the reservation be cut to 1,000 acres chosen by the Secretary of the Interior.
The Band's counsel quotes the Act as requiring the 1,000 acres to be chosen so as not to include the claim of any settler or miner.

breaches.what: Congress took back all but 1,000 acres of the reservation that presidential orders of 1873 and 1874 had set apart for the Southern Paiute; the Secretary's selection followed on July 3, 1875. No consent of the Paiute appears in the record opened.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Act of Congress of March 3, 1875, and order of the Secretary of the Interior of July 3, 1875, as recorded in Royce's schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899)

source.title: Royce, Schedule of Indian Land Cessions, 1874 entries (Moapa reserve)
source.publisher: Bureau of American Ethnology, 18th Annual Report, part 2 (Royce, Indian Land Cessions, 1899), Internet Archive

breaches.what: The Moapa Band's general counsel wrote that the February 12, 1874 order expanded the reservation to well over 2,000,000 acres, that Congress cut it to 1,000 acres in an appropriations rider, and that 99.5% of the reservation was lost when the Secretary made the 1,000-acre selection on July 3, 1875.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Ziontz, Chestnut, Varnell, Berley & Slonim, general counsel to the Moapa Band of Paiutes, letter to the US EPA

source.title: Letter of Ziontz, Chestnut, Varnell, Berley & Slonim, general counsel to the Moapa Band of Paiutes, to the US EPA (May 18, 2004)

breaches.quote: 99.5% of the Reservation was lost to the Tribe at the stroke of a pen

breaches.what: The Southern Paiute claims, including the Moapa band, were settled by compromise before the Indian Claims Commission, which entered a final judgment for the Southern Paiute Nation of $7,253,165.19 under a stipulation of the parties. A compromise is not a finding of breach.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Southern Paiute Nation v. United States, Dockets 88, 330 and 330-A, final judgment on a compromise settlement

source.title: Southern Paiute Nation v. United States, Dockets 88, 330 and 330-A, Final Judgment (January 18, 1965)
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Library, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

compensation: No payment for the 1875 reduction was found. The Southern Paiute claims were settled by compromise for $7,253,165.19 (Indian Claims Commission, January 18, 1965).
today: Congress restored land to the Moapa reservation by Public Law 96-491, signed on December 2, 1980; President Carter's signing statement gives approximately 70,500 acres, and the Band's counsel gives 70,565 acres and a present reservation of about 72,000 acres (letter of May 18, 2004).

nationVoice.summary: Through its general counsel, the Band describes the 1875 reduction as the loss of 99.5% of its reservation, and says the 1980 restoration of about 70,565 acres was meant to redress that loss in part and give it land for development.

openQuestions: The Statutes at Large page for the 1875 reduction was not opened: the Band's counsel cites 18 Stat. 475, while secondary listings cite 18 Stat. 445. Royce gives only 'act of Congress of Mar. 3, 1875'. Confirm against the Statutes at Large before adding a citation.

The record here is an Act, so the breach recorded is the Act itself overriding the reservation orders. A reviewer may prefer to show this Act only as the instrument of the breach on the 1873 and 1874 entries.
